title: Delhi High Court Refuses to Restore Power, Water to Century-Old Race Course Mosque
excerpt: The court dismissed the imam's petition over the October 7 disconnection, as the Waqf Board, the L&DO and the NDMC dispute the heritage mosque's status on government land near the Prime Minister's residence.
body:
• The Delhi High Court has refused to restore electricity and water to the century-old Race Course Masjid near the Prime Minister's residence at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg, after the utilities were disconnected on October 7.
  • The mosque is a Waqf-notified property listed in a 1977 Delhi Gazette notification and a Grade II heritage structure, but the Land and Development Office says the land is government land and the premises are covered by an August 25 eviction judgment.
  • Government sources have said no eviction notice was issued to the mosque itself, even as mosque representatives and news reports describe a six-day notice dated October 19 — the dispute is unresolved.
  • The Delhi Waqf Board has written to the NDMC and the L&DO on October 19 and 21 seeking restoration of power and water for regular prayers.

The Delhi High Court has refused to restore electricity and water to the Race Course Masjid, a century-old mosque near the Prime Minister's residence in New Delhi, dismissing a petition by its imam. According to Maktoob Media's report of the hearing, Justice Saurabh Banerjee held that the imam, Mohd Haroon, had no right to the premises in his personal capacity and therefore could not claim a violation of his fundamental rights over the disconnection.

The mosque stands within the Race Course Club, which spans around 53 acres near 7, Lok Kalyan Marg, behind Safdarjung Tomb. Its electricity and water were disconnected on October 7. Haroon approached the High Court on October 12 seeking restoration.

A heritage structure on contested land

The mosque and its adjoining graveyard appear in the Delhi Administration's Gazette notification dated September 8, 1977, listed under entry number 18 and covering two bighas. The structure is also a Grade II heritage building, notified in 2009, and the Delhi Waqf Board says the mosque has held a lawful electricity connection since 1976. The Board wrote to the NDMC on October 8 saying the connections had been cut without prior notice or apparent valid reason.

https://x.com/MajorPoonia/status/2113627286008471912

The authorities tell a different story. The Land and Development Office (L&DO), which is overseeing the demolition in the area and is set to take possession of the land, maintains that the structure stands on government land. Government sources have said no eviction notice had been issued to the mosque, even as PTI-based reporting described a notice received around October 19 giving the management six days to vacate. That contradiction sits at the centre of the dispute.

"All these are way beyond the scope for this court to adjudicate in the present writ petition."

— Justice Saurabh Banerjee, Delhi High Court

Why the court declined to intervene

The NDMC told the court on October 15 that demolition work, including the removal of jhuggi structures, was still under way in the area and that restoring electricity could pose a risk to public safety. It also argued that the L&DO had not been made a party to Haroon's petition. Although the mosque was not a party to the litigation over the eviction of around 700 slum dwellers and the Race Course Club, the NDMC's counsel told the court orally that the mosque premises were "covered" by a High Court judgment dated August 25, which paved the way for those evictions. The displaced residents have since been rehabilitated in Savda Ghevra, nearly 50 km away.

The court noted that the Waqf Board — described in the order as the "original occupant" of the premises — had not itself challenged the disconnection, and that the petition raised serious disputed questions of fact about Haroon's right, title or interest in the premises and whether the property fell outside the August 25 judgment.

The Waqf Board's position, and the politics

The Delhi Waqf Board has since moved on paper. Its chief executive officer, Tanvir Ahmad, sent letters to the L&DO and the NDMC on October 19 and 21 seeking restoration of both services, citing the 1977 Gazette notification and the connection records dating back to 1976, and saying no legal proceedings were pending against the premises. The Board itself has not been reconstituted since its elected body's tenure ended in August 2023.

The case has drawn political reactions. A Jamiat Ulama-i-Hind delegation met Union Minority Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju on October 19 seeking protection for the mosque and its graveyard, and AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi has urged Rijiju to intervene. Prayers were still being offered at the mosque this week despite the uncertainty, officials said.

What happens next

No demolition of the mosque has been reported, and no final ruling has resolved whether the premises fall inside the August 25 judgment. The next steps rest with the Waqf Board — the body the High Court identified as the occupant with standing to challenge the disconnection — and with the L&DO's possession drive in the Race Course area.
